title: AVN of the Hip: Can the Hip Be Saved, or Do I Need a Hip Replacement?
seoTitle: AVN of the Hip: Save the Hip or Replace It?
metaDescription: Diagnosed with AVN of the hip? Why the stage matters, when core decompression can save the hip, when replacement is needed, and why both hips need an MRI.
intro: Being told you have AVN (avascular necrosis) of the hip is frightening, especially in your 30s or 40s, when hip replacement sounds like something for grandparents. The honest answer to 'do I need a replacement?' is: it depends almost entirely on one thing — whether the ball of the hip has already collapsed. Here is what that means, and what the evidence says about each option.
summary: AVN of the hip is loss of blood supply to the ball of the thighbone. Before the ball collapses, hip-preserving surgery such as core decompression can sometimes save the joint; once it has collapsed, total hip replacement is the most reliable treatment. Early MRI of both hips matters, because the other hip is often affected.

sections.heading: What is AVN of the hip?
sections.body: AVN, also called osteonecrosis, means the blood supply to the ball (femoral head) of the thighbone has been interrupted, so part of the bone dies. Dead bone cannot repair everyday micro-damage, so over months it can weaken and collapse, and the smooth joint surface above it breaks down into arthritis. It usually starts as a dull ache in the groin or buttock, and later hurts with walking and hip movement. AAOS notes that both hips are affected in many cases, and that it is most common between 40 and 65 — though in India we often see it younger.

sections.heading: Why do people get AVN — and is it linked to COVID treatment?
sections.body: The best-known risk factors are corticosteroid (steroid) medicines, heavy alcohol use, and injury such as a hip dislocation or fracture. Conditions such as sickle cell disease and lupus also raise the risk, and in some people no cause is found. After the COVID-19 waves, Indian surgeons reported AVN in young adults who had received steroids during treatment: a 2022 series from Ganga Hospital, Coimbatore, in the Indian Journal of Orthopaedics followed 22 patients (39 hips), with an average age of about 39, whose hip symptoms began on average 7.5 months after COVID infection. That study had no comparison group, so it cannot tell us how common this is — but if you had steroids for COVID, asthma, or any other reason and now have groin pain, mention it to your doctor.

sections.heading: How is AVN diagnosed?
sections.body: An MRI is the key test. In early AVN the X-ray can look completely normal, while an MRI already shows the change in the bone. X-rays then help decide the stage: whether the ball has started to flatten or collapse, and whether the socket is wearing. Because AVN so often affects both hips, we usually image both, even if only one hurts — catching the second hip before it collapses gives it the best chance.

sections.heading: Can AVN be treated without surgery?
sections.body: Medicines, physiotherapy and crutches can ease pain, but there is no good evidence that they stop the disease. A 2019 review in The Permanente Journal states that physiotherapy does not prevent progression, that weight-bearing restrictions have not been shown to prevent it, and that drugs such as bisphosphonates and statins are not proven. Some very small lesions that cause no symptoms can be watched with repeat imaging. For a painful hip, though, waiting is risky: the same review reports that about 80–85% of symptomatic hips go on to collapse within two years.

sections.heading: When can the hip be saved, and when does it need replacing?
sections.body: The deciding question is collapse. Before the ball collapses, hip-preserving surgery — most commonly core decompression, where channels are drilled into the dead bone to relieve pressure and encourage healing, sometimes with bone graft — can prevent progression in some patients. Results vary widely: the Permanente review quotes success rates from 40% to 100% depending on the patients studied, and smaller lesions do better. Once the ball has collapsed, AAOS states that core decompression is not usually successful and that total hip replacement is the most successful treatment.

sections.heading: I'm only 35 — isn't it too early for a hip replacement?
sections.body: Age alone is not a reason to refuse a replacement, and it is not a reason to have one either. If the hip can still be preserved, we try to preserve it. But once the ball has collapsed and pain is limiting walking, sleep and work, delaying usually means years of disability for little gain. Modern total hip replacement relieves pain and restores function in the majority of patients, and implant materials can be chosen with a younger, active patient's lifespan in mind. A replacement may need revising later in life — that is a real trade-off, and worth discussing openly with your surgeon.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor?
sections.body: See an orthopaedic surgeon promptly if you have groin or buttock pain that has lasted more than a few weeks, especially if you have taken steroids, drink heavily, have sickle cell disease, or have had a hip injury. Seek urgent care for sudden severe hip pain after a fall, inability to bear weight, or a hot, swollen hip with fever. Early diagnosis is what keeps hip-saving options open.

faqs.q: Can AVN of the hip heal without surgery?
faqs.a: Medicines, physiotherapy and crutches can ease pain, but there is no good evidence that they stop AVN progressing. Some very small lesions without symptoms can be watched with repeat MRI. Most painful hips progress, so they need assessment early while hip-saving surgery is still an option.

faqs.q: Does AVN always need a hip replacement?
faqs.a: No. If AVN is found before the ball of the hip collapses, hip-preserving surgery such as core decompression can prevent progression in some patients, with better results for smaller lesions. Once the ball has collapsed, total hip replacement is the most reliable treatment.

faqs.q: Can steroids given for COVID cause AVN?
faqs.a: Corticosteroids are a well-known risk factor for AVN, and Indian surgeons have reported AVN in young adults after steroid treatment for COVID, with hip symptoms starting months after the infection. If you received steroids and now have groin pain, tell your doctor; an MRI can detect early AVN.

faqs.q: Will my other hip get AVN too?
faqs.a: It may. AAOS notes that both hips are affected in many cases, and in steroid-related AVN both sides are commonly involved. That is why both hips are usually checked on MRI, even if only one is painful.

Core decompression is a hip-preserving operation in which channels are drilled into the dead area of the femoral head to relieve pressure and encourage new blood supply, sometimes combined with bone graft. It works best before the ball has collapsed; AAOS notes that patients who do well typically walk unassisted in about three months.
